items.title: 35日でフロントエンドの基礎を完全に理解する #34 - 総合演習
items.summary: この記事で学ぶこと いよいよ総合演習です。#1 のブラウザの仕組みから始まり、JavaScript・TypeScript・Vue・テスト・Nuxt・ビルド、そして前回 #33 のモノレポまで、フロントエンドの土台を33回かけて積み上げてきました。 各回の確認テストは「その回の理解」を測るものでした。この総合演習が測るのは違います。複数の回の知識を組み合わせないと解けない、実務でそのまま出会う横断的な問題を用意しました。画面が更新されないバグの切り分け、コードレビューでの指摘、本番だけ遅い画面の調査。どれも「1つの正解を暗記している」だけでは手が動きません。持っている知識をつなげて、根...
items.titleJa: 35日でフロントエンドの基礎を完全に理解する #34 - 総合演習
items.summaryJa: 総合演習では、複数回の知識を横断的に組み合わせて実務的な問題を解く力を問う。遅延画面の原因特定と優先順位づけ、分割コードの適用、非同期のレース対策、型と境界の安全性、データの一方向性と監視の適切な使い方、レビュー時の設計原則など、具体的なシナリオを通じて根拠ある判断と再現性のある修正手順を学ぶ。特に、計測重視の手法、分割代入の罠、最新性を保証するリクエスト管理、境界検査の導入、1箇所に対策を集約する設計、そして不正なデータやXSSなどのセキュリティリスクへの対処が強調されている。

items.titleJa: 隠蔽によるセキュリティって知ってる？

items.titleJa: TypeScriptの有用性を、実際に動かして確かめてみた
items.summaryJa: TypeScriptはJavaScriptに静的な型チェックを加える言語で、主に実行前に型の矛盾を検出する点に有用性があるとした。実際の実験では、型の食い違いやnull処理、打ち間違いの検出など、実行前に指摘されるケースが多い一方、外部から入ってくる値は実行時には型と異なることがあり、型チェックだけでは不完全であると結論づけている。公開情報からも、リファクタリング支援や補完、移行ツールの存在など、導入効果はあるが「型チェックだけで安心できない」点に留意するべきと述べている。

Citations include source URLs, optional titles, and evidence excerpts. They apply to the whole request, rather than mapping individual sources to each answer. items.title: Workflow SDK 5: built for production
items.summary: When we first launched Workflow SDK, the goal was simple: write regular async JavaScript, and let the SDK keep it running through crashes, deployments, and long waits. Last year, we shipped just that , with the world-class developer experience Vercel is known for. Then we watched what our customers built with it. More than 4 billion steps and 700 million runs later, two clear patterns have emerged. The first is automation : Traditional workflows that move data, process orders, coordinate background jobs, manage subscriptions, and run ETL and data pipelines. The second is agents and harnesses : Agents are expensive and long running, so they naturally require durability too. As those workloads matured, Workflow matured with them. Our priorities have always been security, reliability, and performance. Here’s how Workflow SDK 5 delivers on all three. More secure workflows The Workflow event log stores step arguments and return values so a run can recover after a crash or deployment. That data can include sensitive customer information, model context, credentials, and tool-call results. Persisting it requires strong protection. Workflow SDK encrypts every payload end to end , before it leaves your code. Workflow and step inputs and outputs, hook payloads, and stream data are encrypted with AES-256-GCM, using a unique key for each run. With encryption enabled, any Workflow SDK backend, including Vercel, only sees and stores ciphertext. Plaintext is decrypted in your deployment or in authorized observability tools. Encryption with zero configuration on Vercel On Vercel, encryption needs no setup and no code changes. Each run’s key is derived from a key scoped to the deployment that created it, so a run can only decrypt its own data. Your workflow code doesn’t change: Because Vercel manages the keys by default, observability keeps working. Names, timings, and statuses are always visible, and when you need to see a payload, you can decrypt it in the dashboard or the CLI. Decryption happens in your browser or terminal, follows the same permissions as the project’s environment variables, and every request is recorded in your team’s audit log. Encryption on self-hosted Worlds Encryption is implemented in the SDK, so it can also protect payloads on self-hosted Worlds before they reach storage, queues, or streams. A custom World enables encryption by implementing getEncryptionKeyForRun() with your key management . Return the same 32-byte key for each run on every call so the SDK can encrypt new payloads and decrypt them during replay: More security work in v5 Cross-run writes are sealed too. When code resumes another run’s hook, starts a run in another deployment, or writes into a stream forwarded from another run, the payload is encrypted to the target run’s public key. The writer can encrypt for that run without reading its existing payloads. You can also limit how long sensitive data is stored. With payload retention set to experimental_retention: 0 , inputs, outputs, and stream contents are deleted as soon as a run completes or fails. The run’s metadata stays visible in observability. A redesigned trace viewer The redesigned trace viewer makes runs easier to navigate, with span search, zoom, a minimap, and local inspection during development. Run attributes are new in v5. They let you attach searchable context to a run, such as an order ID, and then find runs by it. Attributes are plaintext, so they should not contain secrets. Workflows in every region In Workflow SDK 4, every run lived in iad1 . Even when a project was deployed to several regions, each run’s event log, queue, and streams were only stored in one region, so a step running anywhere else made cross-region requests to record its progress. For v5, we deployed Workflow infrastructure to every Vercel Function region . Each run has its own home region: its state, queue dispatch, and streams are served from the region where it started, without cross-region round trips on the hot path. By default, a run starts in the region of the function that starts it. Deploy to several regions, and each run stays close to the user who triggered it, with no configuration: To place a run somewhere else, pass a region to start() . That lets a workflow run next to the database it reads and writes, or keep a customer’s data in the region where it has to stay: The region option decides where a run’s data lives. Your steps run where your app is deployed, so deploy to that region too if you want them to execute there. Existing v4 runs stay in iad1 . Infrastructure reliability Regional isolation also improves reliability. A disruption in one region does not have to stop new runs in healthy regions. For projects with Vercel Function failover configured, steps can execute in a fallback region while continuing to use the run’s original home region for state. That state remains pinned to its home region; it does not migrate during failover. With the help of anonymized telemetry and close collaboration with many customers, we found and fixed dozens of rare bugs and race conditions in the Workflow runtime. Workflow SDK also recovers on its own from more kinds of intermittent network errors. As a result, with Workflow SDK 5, we’ve seen almost no runs fail or stall because of a platform or runtime bug. Agent-ready performance In Workflow SDK 4, every step invocation involved a queue hop to start the step and another to continue the workflow. That is acceptable for slow background automations, but adds latency to the AI workloads developers are building today. Agent loops and harnesses can contain thousands of sequential events, high-throughput token streams, tool chains, and dynamic subagents. At that scale, the networking and CPU work around every step became a limit. In Workflow SDK 5, we rewrote large parts of the engine to minimize extra queue hops, unnecessary networking, and CPU work. Across the measured workloads, we saw 1.6× to 25× improvements in measured latency and overhead, while preserving the same developer experience and introducing no major breaking changes. The benchmarks below compare v5.2.0 with v4.8.12 on Vercel. Pick a measurement to see how v5 compares with v4, then play or scrub through the explainer to see exactly what each benchmark measures. Workflow SDK 5 includes hundreds of performance improvements to achieve this. Here are some of the major changes behind these numbers: Fewer queue hops In v4, each step handed execution back through the queue. In v5, an invocation can execute several steps inline, including parallel steps, before yielding for a wait, a hook, or an approaching timeout. The runtime also avoids unnecessary persistence round trips and folds step creation into execution. Fewer queue and network requests mean less CPU work and lower runtime overhead. In a five-step benchmark, p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 618 ms to 109 ms . Incremental replay Over a 1,020-step benchmark, v4’s p75 overhead grew with the event log : replaying the full event history took time proportional to its size. In the final sampled range, overhead reached 1,748 ms. On v5.2.0, it was 70 ms . The median time to finish all 1,020 steps fell from 21.0 minutes to 3.0 minutes. WebSocket streaming Durability should not make a streamed response fall behind its producer. On the Vercel World, v5.2.0 writes streams over WebSockets by default . In a benchmark replaying a 52.4-second agent response, median delivery dropped from 226.1 seconds to 53.5 seconds . Payload compression reduces the data stored and transferred. AI token streams average around 80% smaller after compression. These measurements describe one workload, in one region, against the Vercel World. They are a useful view of runtime overhead, rather than a prediction for every application. Benchmark results and methodology Measured October 8, 2026, on Vercel production in iad1 , against the managed Vercel World . Each version uses a separate deployment of the same app. Steps take 1 KB of JSON in and out. Selected results · v4.8.12 compared with v5.2.0 Measurement v4.8.12 v5.2.0 Change First step, p75 418 ms 172 ms 2.4× faster Between steps, p75 618 ms 109 ms 5.7× faster Late-run overhead, p75 1,748 ms 70 ms 25× lower 1,020 steps, median 21.0 min 3.0 min 7× faster Resume, p75 699 ms 425 ms 1.6× faster Stream delivery, median 226.1 s 53.5 s 4.2× faster Chunk trip time, p75 172 ms 102 ms 1.7× faster Runs with a chunk delayed >1 s 6 / 10 0 / 10 100% fewer The full results, including tails, are in the performance documentation . Worlds: the shared durability primitive Workflow SDK’s durable functions sit on a World : the interface for storing progress, dispatching work, and delivering streams. That same foundation also now supports fx and durable-harness , which adds durability to existing agent harnesses. Improvements to the shared storage, queue, and streaming infrastructure can benefit any consumer of a World. Optimizations inside the Workflow replay runtime apply to Workflow SDK; they do not automatically apply to every harness. Choose the integration around how you want to build: Workflow SDK : write durable application logic with use workflow and use step . WorkflowAgent : use @ai-sdk/workflow for an AI SDK agent loop inside a workflow. fx : embed and extend a native coding agent with libfx. durable-harness : keep an existing supported harness and add durability beneath it. Supports Pi and OpenCode , with experimental integrations for Claude Code and Codex in Vercel Sandbox. eve : build agents with durable sessions powered natively by Workflow SDK and Worlds. We’ll soon be adding more offerings to our catalog of SDKs and frameworks backed by Worlds for durability. Build with Workflow SDK 5 Besides the improvements above, Workflow SDK 5 also adds: In-flight cancellation with AbortController Searchable run attributes More framework integrations And more The v5 upgrade docs cover what changed. To start building a new workflow, install the SDK: Workflow SDK also has a Python SDK , now in beta, with the same durable workflows, steps, sleeps, and hooks. Read more

Nami Poursafargholi 🔡 Tinkerfont: A Font Inspection and Switching Tool for Chrome & Firefox — Install this extension and you get a quick way to inspect fonts on the current page (and their properties), and try alternative fonts directly on the page. Mighil BagUI: Components & Blocks for Building SaaS Landing Pages — A free collection that includes clean, customizable marketing pages, app pages, blocks, and templates for React and shadcn/ui users. Source code . Anelka Bagalane Master CSS 2.0: A Markup-Driven CSS Language — A utility-class framework where one class can carry a value, selector and condition (e.g. fg-blue-70:hover@sm ). v2 adds design tokens defined in your own CSS, a wide-gamut color palette, and linting and editor tooling. Aoyue Design 📰 Classifieds 🔁 Your agent checks web work with a refresh. On mobile it needs a device. Expo Simulators gives it one in the cloud. 📅 Booking forms without a backend : Real availability, live totals and deposits via your own Stripe or PayPal. CraftForms, from €6/month . ✍️ Foxit : Still redirecting users to a signing portal? 6 eSignature APIs compared on embedded signing, pricing and integration effort. 🛑 Finally, if you want to keep the bots out … A Blunt Banhammer Blocks Basic Bots Ballistically — Terence Eden's site was plagued by bots using up his bandwidth, so he built an interesting honeypot that lures the robots.txt -ignoring bots in and hands out a ban. It works, with an almost 90% drop in bandwidth used, but there are some tradeoffs. If you're happy to lean on the cloud for protection, Nick Gray recounts his year of fighting scrapers with Cloudflare , including his firewall rules and failed experiments. Meanwhile, with a more… 'creative' approach, Utku Sen filled a test site's code with taboo phrases and found AI agents refused to touch it . This may be more useful if you want to prevent casual reverse engineering/vulnerability hunting, though. Finally, even if you welcome crawlers, they can make your analytics misleading. Hugo Attal looked into his server logs and found 90% of his 'human' visitors were bots . Till next time…

items.titleJa: CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today?

items.title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
items.summary: AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026 Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August , September , and October . November 2026 Summary In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July. OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one . OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December. More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on. Decision models account for 26% of all requests Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive. Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model. They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model. Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend. Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models. Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did. This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively. Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%. New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%. Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July. A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps: A voice model turns the user’s speech into text A language model writes the reply Another voice model reads the reply back to the user Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled. Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped. For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both. Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54. Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five. Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI. But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets. On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period. Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten. Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models. Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab. Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens. AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one. Also in October’s data Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two. Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten. OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0. About this data This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026. A few notes on measurement: Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month. Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list. Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025. Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens. Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day. A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month. All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated. Read more about our methodology , and explore or download the public data . items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 now available on AI Gateway
items.summary: Claude Fable 5.2 from Anthropic is now available on AI Gateway . Fable 5.2 is built for open-ended technical work and improves on earlier Fable models in coding, reasoning, and vision. It can run long, ambiguous tasks unattended, and works as an orchestrator that hands simpler tasks to smaller models, or as an advisor that other Claude models consult on harder problems. It also communicates more clearly and generates output faster than earlier Fable models. Effort runs from low to max , with high as the API default. Fable 5.2 has cybersecurity and biology safety classifiers enabled. Access to Claude Fable 5.2 requires data retention. Anthropic does not support Zero Data Retention for the model. Prompts and completions are retained for 30 days and are not used to train Claude. If your team has ZDR turned on, AI Gateway returns an error instead of sending the request to Fable 5.2. To keep requests served when a classifier is triggered, use model fallbacks . Add a models array to providerOptions.gateway , and AI Gateway tries each model in order when the cybersecurity classifier declines a request. Call it through the AI SDK , the Chat Completions , Responses , and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. Use anthropic/claude-fable-5.2 as the model name: This request falls back to Opus 5.5, then Sonnet 5.5, if the cybersecurity classifier declines it. The models option works the same way on every AI Gateway API format. To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Try Claude Fable 5.2 in the model playground . items.title: Muse Ember now available on AI Gateway
items.summary: Muse Ember from Meta is now available on AI Gateway . It is a lightweight reasoning model for the high-volume parts of an agent run, such as coding sub-tasks, tool calls, and document analysis. Muse Ember handles the bounded tasks agents repeat many times in a single run, like implementing a helper function, calling a tool, or summarizing a document. The model accepts text, image, and video input with a 1M-token context window, so an agent can pass it code, screenshots, documents, and clips in the same run. Tool calling lets your application feed each result into the next step. Reasoning effort is adjustable from minimal to max . Call it through the AI SDK , the Chat Completions , Responses , and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway.
